#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""skills-lint.py [FILE...]: find the coordinator's agenda in the project skills.

The patterns and their scopes are the "Lint pattern list" of
explorations/reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md:

  fortress-repo and cloud-container, SKILL.md and parts: every set but sources;
  coordinator, SKILL.md and parts: handles (coordinator form), status, stale;
  every references/sources.md: the sources set only.

A file's skill is the folder after "skills/" in its path, so a copy made with
`git show REV:.claude/skills/...` into a folder of the same layout is linted
as the file it copies. A skill not named above takes every set.

With no FILE, every file under the repository's .claude/skills/. Prints
`path:line: set: text` for each hit, the text clipped around the match, and
exits 1 if there is any. Patterns are case-insensitive unless they say (?-i:...).
ALLOW lists hits read and passed, by file, set and a substring of the line.
"""
import os, re, sys

HANDLES = [
    r"\bQ\d+(\.\d+)?\b",
    r"\bitems? (1\d|[2-9]\d|\d{3})[a-z]?\b",
    r"\b(climb )?batch(es)? \d+('s)?\b",
    r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b|\brung's\b",
    r"\b(review|gather|coldread|delta-unfolded|review-routed|judge-review)\.\d+\b",
]
HANDLES_COORDINATOR = HANDLES[:3] + [r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b"]
STATUS = [
    r"\b(pending|unanswered|not (yet )?answered|has not answered|awaiting|still open|leaves the question|to be applied)\b",
    r"\bdoes not yet say\b|\b(is|are) not yet (decided|known|answered)\b",
    r"\bthe default of (Q\d|item \d|way)|\bat (its|the) default\b|\bway \d+[a-z]?\b",
]
PROVENANCE = [
    r"\bcurator('s)? (decided|kept|chose|ruled|answered)\b",
    r"\bthe curator (gives|weighs|keeps)\b",
    r"\bcurator's (answer|decision|ruling|choice)\b",
    r"\bis a decision of the curator\b",
    r"\b(his|her) (answer|decision|word|go|review|choice)\b",

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the run time. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	## The library order
74	
75	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76	
77	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78	
79	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81	
82	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
86	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
87	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
90	
91	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
92	
93	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
94	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
95	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
96	
97	## Name resolution
98	
99	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
100	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
101	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
102	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
103	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
104	
105	## Building
106	
107	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
108	
109	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
110	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
111	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
113	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
114	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
115	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
116	
117	## After an edit of the library
118	
119	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
120	
121	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
122	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
123	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
124	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
125	
126	## Symptoms of a skipped step
127	
128	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
129	
130	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
131	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
132	
133	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
134	
135	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
136	
137	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
138	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
139	
140	Two more facts help you read a run:
141	
142	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
143	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
144

1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
2	
3	**prompt cache**
4	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
5	
6	**interrupt**
7	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
8	
9	**stop of the process**
10	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
11	
12	**automatic permission check**
13	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
14	
15	## The Bash tool and waits
16	
17	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
18	
19	- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
20	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
21	
22	## Long commands
23	
24	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
25	
26	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
27	
28	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
29	
30	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
31	
32	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
33	
34	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
35	        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
36	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
37	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
38	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
39	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
40	        done
41	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
42	    }
43	
44	## Stopping processes
45	
46	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
47	
48	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
49	
50	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
51	
52	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
53	
54	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
55	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
56	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
57	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
58	
59	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
60	
61	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
62	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
63

1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
44	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
45	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
46	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
47	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
48	
49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
65	
66	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
72

1	# The gate
2	
3	The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.
4	
5	## What it writes
6	
7	The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
8	
9	If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.
10	
11	Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:
12	
13	    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh
14	
15	## When to run it
16	
17	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
18	
19	If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:
20	
21	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
22	    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
23	        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'
24	
25	- If it prints a path, run the gate.
26	- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).
27	
28	## The steps
29	
30	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.
31	
32	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
33	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
34	3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:
35	
36	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
37	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
38	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine
39	
40	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
41	5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
42	6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
43	7. Do the ladder regression.
44	
45	## The atomic runs
46	
47	The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
48	
49	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
50	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
51	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
52	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
53	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
54	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
55	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
56	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
57	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
58	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
59	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
60	      done
61	    done
62	
63	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
64	
65	## The ladder regression
66	
67	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
68	
69	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
70	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
71	
72	A file that moved gets a mark:
73	
74	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
75	- MISSING: a file with no output.
76	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
77	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
78	
79	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
80	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
81	
82	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
83	
84	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
85	
86	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
87	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
88	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
89	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
90	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
91	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
92	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
93	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
94	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
95	
96	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
97	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
98	
99	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
100	
101	## Comparing with an earlier run
102	
103	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
104	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
105	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.
106

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	Three limits of `ledger.py` (below):
55	
56	- A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no further note.
57	- No command edits a row's claim. `close --claim` takes a corrected one.
58	- Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
59	
60	## Reading the record
61	
62	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
63	
64	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
65	
66	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
67	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
68	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
69	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
70	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
71	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
72	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
73	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
74	
75	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
76	
77	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
78	
79	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
80	
81	## Writing to the record
82	
83	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
84	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
85	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
86	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
87	  - what it means for the work;
88	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
89	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
90	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
91	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
92	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
93	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
94	
95	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
96	
97	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
98	
99	To add a row:
100	
101	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
102	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
103	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
104	
105	To change a row:
106	
107	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
108	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
109	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: coordinator
3	description: "Use this skill in the Fortress revival's coordinating session whenever the curator (who decides what is committed and what agents do) is directing you, waiting on you, or setting how the conversation goes. Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Load it too when they say they will review your turns one by one, ask you to hold or restate something, keep quiet during a batch, or change your register or format. Load it before briefing, launching, resuming or relaunching agents, picking a tier, estimating tokens, or editing FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the review queue, boot note or held list. Not for workers, build/test work (fortress-repo), container or hook faults (cloud-container), or generic multi-agent or ADR questions."
4	---
5	
6	# The coordinating session
7	
8	You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.
9	
10	**curator**
11	: Person in charge of this restoration.
12	
13	**worker**
14	: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.
15	
16	**record**
17	: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.
18	
19	**entry**
20	: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.
21	
22	**batch**
23	: Run of the batch workflow script (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs. A rung is one task of it, with its own worker and worktree.
24	
25	**land**
26	: Commit a batch's merged work to `main` and push it.
27	
28	**model program**
29	: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured.
30	
31	**fork**
32	: Design question with more than one way forward.
33	
34	**cross-area question**
35	: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.
36	
37	**go**
38	: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.
39	
40	**ask**
41	: Message that puts one decision to the curator.
42	
43	**hold**
44	: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.
45	
46	**review list**
47	: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: items for the curator's later review.
48	
49	**interrupt**
50	: Stop of a turn by the stop button.
51	
52	**process stop**
53	: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.
54	
55	**tokens written**
56	: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.
57	
58	**boot note**
59	: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.
60	
61	**held list**
62	: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.
63	
64	## The standing goal
65	
66	You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.
67	
68	- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
69	- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
70	- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
71	
72	## The curator's role and decisions
73	
74	The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
75	
76	Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. They settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
77	
78	A decision is consequential if it:
79	
80	- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
81	- touches microGPT: a line of the model program, its speed or its readability;
82	- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
83	- or cannot be undone.
84	
85	It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
86	
87	1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
88	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
89	3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
90	
91	Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
92	
93	- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
94	- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
95	- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
96	- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
97	- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
98	- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
99	- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
100	- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
101	
102	## The facts of this environment
103	
104	- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
105	- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
106	- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
107	- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
108	- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
109	- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
110	- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
111	- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
112	- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
113	- The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn. Its reminders are advisory.
114	- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
115	- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
116	- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.
117	
118	## Talking to the curator
119	
120	- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
121	- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
122	- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
123	- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
124	- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
125	- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
126	- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
127	- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
128	- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
129	- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
130	- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
131	
132	**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:
133	
134	1. The question, in one line.
135	2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example: why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it.
136	3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs.
137	4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
138	5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
139	
140	Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
141	
142	**Quiet times.**
143	
144	- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
145	- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone, or after a process stop the hook's one line.
146	- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
147	- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end or a hold. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
148	
149	**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. Your default, an answer to each point as it comes, buries the curator in text.
150	
151	- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
152	- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
153	- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing.
154	- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
155	
156	**Pages.**
157	
158	- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
159	- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
160	- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
161	- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
162	- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
163	- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
164	
165	## The record: what goes where
166	
167	Under `explorations/coordinator/`:
168	
169	- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
170	- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
171	- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
172	- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
173	- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
174	- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under the landing that moved them.
175	- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages.
176	- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
177	- `review-queue.md`: the review lists, sorted by theme.
178	
179	Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.
180	
181	FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.
182	
183	- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
184	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
185	- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
186	- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
187	- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.
188	
189	## The boot
190	
191	At session start and after each compaction, read these in order:
192	
193	1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
194	2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
195	3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
196	4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
197	5. The boot note, then the held list.
198	6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
199	7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
200	
201	- Read nothing else. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
202	- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
203	- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
204	- After each process stop, tell the curator in one line that the git-check hook is back on. Only the curator can turn it off again, by switching the session to manual mode (`cloud-container`, its hooks part).
205	
206	## The parts
207	
208	- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
209	- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
210	- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
211	- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX or a history file.
212	- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
213	- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
214	- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.
215

1	# Running and reviewing a batch
2	
3	The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.
4	
5	**batch record**
6	: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<name>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.
7	
8	**base**
9	: Commit that the batch starts from.
10	
11	**gather**
12	: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.
13	
14	**merged-diff review**
15	: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.
16	
17	**repair round**
18	: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.
19	
20	**commit stage**
21	: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.
22	
23	**reserved point**
24	: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.
25	
26	**checker count**
27	: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.
28	
29	**distance**
30	: All the checker's errors on that library, which must reach zero before the switch-over: the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.
31	
32	## The go
33	
34	- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
35	- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
36	- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.
37	
38	## The workflow
39	
40	- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
41	- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
42	- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
43	- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
44	- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
45	- At each landing, report the share of agents that read the briefing in their first turn. Aim for about 80 percent, the share it once had; it fell to 25 to 35.
46	
47	## The roles
48	
49	- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder.
50	- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
51	- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
52	- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.
53	
54	## The checker count and the distance
55	
56	The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.
57	
58	- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
59	- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
60	- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
61	- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.
62	
63	## Reserved points and repairs
64	
65	- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
66	- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
67	- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
68	- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
69	- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
70	
71	## While it runs
72	
73	- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the boot note, and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
74	- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
75	- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.
76	
77	## The landing
78	
79	1. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
80	2. Have the writer update `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
81	3. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
82	4. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
83	5. File what the review finds in PLAN. Move each item that the batch built or answered, and each stale item, word for word into `PLAN-history.md`. An open item whose text stands in another home becomes one line in PLAN, with a pointer to that home. The manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing", step 2, gives the headings and the line's form.
84

51 explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md
<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."
